meta.titre: Hydrogen Bonding: from boiling points of hydrides to solubility and the density of ice

sections.contenu_markdown: A sachet of pure water left in a cooler in Douala stays liquid all afternoon at 30 °C, yet hydrogen sulphide, a molecule almost twice as heavy, escapes as a gas at room temperature. Water is not special because of its size. It is special because its molecules are held together by hydrogen bonds. The same attractions explain why ethanol mixes with water in a bottle of local gin, why ice floats on a pond and why alcohols boil at much higher temperatures than amines or ethers of similar mass. At GCE Advanced Level, hydrogen bonding is behind many questions on boiling points, solubility and the density of ice, and examiners expect a precise definition and a correct comparison, not the vague phrase "water has strong bonds".

items: Electronegativity is the power of an atom to attract the bonding pair of electrons in a covalent bond; nitrogen, oxygen and fluorine are the most electronegative common elements.
A covalent bond between atoms of different electronegativity is polar: the more electronegative atom carries a partial negative charge $\delta-$ and the other a partial positive charge $\delta+$.
Instantaneous dipole-induced dipole (van der Waals) forces act between all molecules and become stronger as the number of electrons in the molecule increases.
Melting and boiling a molecular substance overcome the forces between molecules; the covalent bonds inside the molecules are not broken.

sections.titre: What a hydrogen bond is, when it forms and what it explains
sections.contenu_markdown:
**Definition.** A hydrogen bond is a strong permanent dipole-dipole attraction between a hydrogen atom carrying a partial positive charge $\delta+$, which is covalently bonded to nitrogen, oxygen or fluorine, and a lone pair of electrons on a nitrogen, oxygen or fluorine atom of a neighbouring molecule. It is drawn as a dotted line, $\mathrm{X-H\cdots Y}$, where X and Y are each N, O or F. It is an attraction between molecules, not a covalent bond inside a molecule.

**Two conditions must both be met.**

1. The hydrogen atom must be bonded directly to N, O or F. These atoms are small and strongly electronegative, so the hydrogen is left almost as a bare proton with a large $\delta+$ charge.
2. The molecule receiving the bond must offer a lone pair on N, O or F.

So $\mathrm{CH_4}$ and $\mathrm{HCl}$ form no hydrogen bonds, and pure propanone has none either: its oxygen has lone pairs but there is no O-H bond. Propanone can, however, accept hydrogen bonds from water.

**Strength.** A hydrogen bond is much weaker than a covalent bond (the O-H bond in water is about 460 kJ per mole, a hydrogen bond between water molecules is roughly 20 kJ per mole) but clearly stronger than the van der Waals forces between small molecules.

**Evidence from boiling points of hydrides.**

| Group | Boiling points of the hydrides / °C |
|---|---|
| 14 | CH4 -162, SiH4 -112, GeH4 -88, SnH4 -52 |
| 15 | NH3 -33, PH3 -88, AsH3 -62, SbH3 -17 |
| 16 | H2O 100, H2S -60, H2Se -41, H2Te -2 |
| 17 | HF 20, HCl -85, HBr -67, HI -35 |

Down Group 14 the boiling point rises smoothly because van der Waals forces grow with the number of electrons. In Groups 15, 16 and 17 the first hydride ($\mathrm{NH_3}$, $\mathrm{H_2O}$, HF) is far above the trend: hydrogen bonds add to the van der Waals forces.

**Consequences.**

- High melting and boiling points compared with molecules of similar mass.
- Solubility in water: small molecules that can form hydrogen bonds with water (ammonia, alcohols, amines, carboxylic acids) dissolve well, because the bonds formed with water compensate the bonds broken.
- Ice is less dense than liquid water: in ice each molecule is hydrogen-bonded to four others in an open lattice with empty spaces; on melting some bonds break and the molecules pack more closely.

variantes.nom: Why water boils higher than hydrogen fluoride
variantes.quand_utiliser: When two hydrides both show hydrogen bonding and you must compare their boiling points
variantes.contenu_markdown:
Fluorine is more electronegative than oxygen, so each single hydrogen bond in HF is the stronger one. What decides the boiling point of the liquid is the **average number of hydrogen bonds per molecule**, which is limited by the number of hydrogen atoms available to act as donors and the number of lone pairs available as acceptors.

- HF: one hydrogen and three lone pairs, so on average only one hydrogen bond per molecule (zig-zag chains).
- $\mathrm{H_2O}$: two hydrogens and two lone pairs, so on average two hydrogen bonds per molecule (a three-dimensional network).
- $\mathrm{NH_3}$: three hydrogens but only one lone pair, so about one bond per molecule, and N is less electronegative than O or F, so each bond is weaker.

Hence the order of boiling points is $\mathrm{H_2O} > \mathrm{HF} > \mathrm{NH_3}$.

variantes.nom: Alcohols, amines and ethers of similar relative molecular mass
variantes.quand_utiliser: When asked to rank compounds that have almost the same mass but different functional groups
variantes.contenu_markdown:
| Compound | $M_r$ | Boiling point / °C | Intermolecular forces |
|---|---|---|---|
| Methoxyethane, $\mathrm{CH_3OCH_2CH_3}$ | 60.0 | 7 | van der Waals and weak permanent dipole-dipole; no O-H, so no hydrogen bonding |
| Propan-1-amine, $\mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH_2NH_2}$ | 59.0 | 48 | $\mathrm{N-H\cdots N}$ hydrogen bonds (weaker, N is less electronegative than O) |
| Propan-1-ol, $\mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH_2OH}$ | 60.0 | 97 | $\mathrm{O-H\cdots O}$ hydrogen bonds (stronger, O is more electronegative than N) |

A primary amine therefore boils lower than the alcohol of similar mass, but higher than the ether and the alkane, which cannot form hydrogen bonds between their own molecules.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When a carboxylic acid gives an unexpectedly high boiling point or an apparent relative molecular mass that is too large
variantes.contenu_markdown: Two molecules of ethanoic acid, $\mathrm{CH_3COOH}$, join through **two** hydrogen bonds, $\mathrm{O-H\cdots O=C}$, to form a ring-shaped dimer. In the vapour and in a non-polar solvent such as benzene the acid is largely present as dimers, so its apparent relative molecular mass is close to 120 instead of 60.0. Because of these strong double links, ethanoic acid (boiling point 118 °C) boils much higher than ethanol (78 °C, $M_r = 46.0$), and carboxylic acids boil higher than alcohols of similar mass.

sections.enonce_markdown: Ethanol, $\mathrm{CH_3CH_2OH}$, and methoxymethane, $\mathrm{CH_3OCH_3}$, have the same molecular formula. Ethanol boils at 78 °C and methoxymethane at -24 °C. (a) Show that the two compounds have the same relative molecular mass. (b) Explain the large difference in boiling point. (c) Explain why ethanol mixes with water in all proportions. (H = 1.0, C = 12.0, O = 16.0)

etapes.action: Calculate the relative molecular mass of each compound.
etapes.justification: Both are isomers with formula $\mathrm{C_2H_6O}$, so one calculation covers both.

etapes.action: Identify the intermolecular forces in each liquid.
etapes.justification: In ethanol the oxygen atom carries a hydrogen (an O-H bond); in methoxymethane the oxygen is bonded to two carbon atoms and no hydrogen is attached to it.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Ethanol: hydrogen bonds $\mathrm{O-H\cdots O}$, plus van der Waals forces. Methoxymethane: van der Waals forces and weak permanent dipole-dipole attractions only.

etapes.action: Compare the energy needed to separate the molecules.
etapes.justification: With equal $M_r$ the van der Waals forces are similar, so the difference comes from the hydrogen bonds, which are much stronger than dipole-dipole attractions.
etapes.resultat_markdown: More energy is needed to overcome the hydrogen bonds in ethanol, so ethanol has the higher boiling point (78 °C against -24 °C).

etapes.action: Explain the miscibility of ethanol with water.
etapes.justification: Ethanol has an O-H group that can donate a hydrogen bond to the oxygen of water, and its oxygen lone pairs can accept hydrogen bonds from the hydrogen atoms of water.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Hydrogen bonds $\mathrm{C_2H_5O-H\cdots OH_2}$ and $\mathrm{H-O-H\cdots O(H)C_2H_5}$ form between ethanol and water; the energy released compensates the energy needed to break the hydrogen bonds in pure ethanol and in pure water, so the two mix freely.

sections.conclusion_markdown: Equal relative molecular masses give similar van der Waals forces; the O-H bond of ethanol, absent in methoxymethane, allows hydrogen bonding, which raises the boiling point and gives complete miscibility with water.

items.erreur_markdown: "In a water molecule the hydrogen bond is the bond between H and O."
items.pourquoi_faux: The bond between H and O inside one water molecule is a covalent bond. A hydrogen bond is an attraction between two different molecules.
items.correction_markdown: The covalent bond is $\mathrm{O-H}$ (within a molecule). The hydrogen bond is $\mathrm{O-H\cdots O}$ between a hydrogen of one molecule and the oxygen of another. When water boils, hydrogen bonds break, not covalent bonds.

items.erreur_markdown: "Methane contains hydrogen, so $\mathrm{CH_4}$ molecules form hydrogen bonds."
items.pourquoi_faux: A hydrogen bond needs hydrogen bonded to N, O or F. In methane the hydrogen is bonded to carbon, which is not electronegative enough to leave a large $\delta+$ on H, and there is no lone pair to receive the bond.
items.correction_markdown: Methane has only van der Waals forces. Check for an N-H, O-H or F-H bond and a lone pair on N, O or F before claiming hydrogen bonding.

items.erreur_markdown: "HI has the highest boiling point among the hydrogen halides because it has the strongest hydrogen bonding."
items.pourquoi_faux: Hydrogen bonding is strongest in HF; iodine is not electronegative enough to form hydrogen bonds. HI is higher than HCl and HBr only because of its larger number of electrons.
items.correction_markdown: Boiling points: HF 20 °C, HCl -85 °C, HBr -67 °C, HI -35 °C. HF is high because of hydrogen bonding; from HCl to HI the increase is due to van der Waals forces.

items.erreur_markdown: "Water boils at a higher temperature than HF because oxygen is more electronegative than fluorine."
items.pourquoi_faux: Fluorine is the more electronegative element, so the individual hydrogen bond in HF is stronger. The argument reverses the facts.
items.correction_markdown: Water has two hydrogens and two lone pairs per molecule, so it forms on average two hydrogen bonds per molecule; HF forms about one. More bonds per molecule outweigh the greater strength of each HF bond.

items.erreur_markdown: "Propanone has an oxygen with lone pairs, so liquid propanone is hydrogen-bonded."
items.pourquoi_faux: Liquid propanone has no hydrogen bonded to oxygen (or N or F) to act as the donor, so its molecules cannot form hydrogen bonds with one another.
items.correction_markdown: Propanone has permanent dipole-dipole and van der Waals forces only. It dissolves in water because water molecules donate hydrogen bonds to the oxygen of propanone.

items.enonce_markdown: Which of these substances can form hydrogen bonds between their own molecules: $\mathrm{CH_3F}$, $\mathrm{CH_3OH}$, $\mathrm{CH_3NH_2}$, $\mathrm{CH_3OCH_3}$, $\mathrm{HCl}$, $\mathrm{C_2H_6}$? Give a reason for each answer.
items.solution_markdown:
A hydrogen bond between identical molecules needs an H atom bonded to N, O or F **and** a lone pair on N, O or F.

- $\mathrm{CH_3F}$: F has lone pairs but H is bonded to C only. **No.**
- $\mathrm{CH_3OH}$: has an O-H bond and lone pairs on O. **Yes.**
- $\mathrm{CH_3NH_2}$: has N-H bonds and a lone pair on N. **Yes.**
- $\mathrm{CH_3OCH_3}$: O has lone pairs but no H is attached to O. **No.**
- $\mathrm{HCl}$: H is bonded to Cl, which is not N, O or F. **No.**
- $\mathrm{C_2H_6}$: only C-H bonds and no lone pair. **No.**

**Only $\mathrm{CH_3OH}$ and $\mathrm{CH_3NH_2}$ form hydrogen bonds between their own molecules.**

items.enonce_markdown: Data are given for three compounds. Butane, $\mathrm{C_4H_{10}}$: boiling point -1 °C. Propanone, $\mathrm{CH_3COCH_3}$: boiling point 56 °C. Propan-1-ol, $\mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH_2OH}$: boiling point 97 °C. (H = 1.0, C = 12.0, O = 16.0) (a) Calculate the relative molecular mass of each compound. (b) State the strongest type of intermolecular force in each liquid and explain why the boiling points differ although the masses are similar.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) Butane: $M_r = 4\times12.0 + 10\times1.0 = 58.0$. Propanone: $3\times12.0 + 6\times1.0 + 16.0 = 58.0$. Propan-1-ol: $3\times12.0 + 8\times1.0 + 16.0 = 60.0$.

(b) The masses are almost equal, so van der Waals forces are of similar size in all three. The differences come from the additional forces.

- Butane: non-polar, only instantaneous dipole-induced dipole forces. Lowest boiling point, -1 °C.
- Propanone: polar C=O bond gives permanent dipole-dipole attractions; no H is bonded to O, so no hydrogen bonds between its molecules. Intermediate, 56 °C.
- Propan-1-ol: contains an O-H bond, so molecules form $\mathrm{O-H\cdots O}$ hydrogen bonds. Highest, 97 °C.

**Order of increasing boiling point: butane < propanone < propan-1-ol**, following the increasing strength of the strongest intermolecular force (van der Waals, dipole-dipole, hydrogen bonding).

items.enonce_markdown: (Use $N_A = 6.02\times10^{23}\ \mathrm{mol^{-1}}$, H = 1.0, O = 16.0, F = 19.0.) In ice each water molecule is hydrogen-bonded to four neighbours, and every hydrogen bond is shared between two molecules. In liquid hydrogen fluoride, assume that each molecule takes part in two hydrogen bonds, each shared between two molecules. (a) Calculate the number of hydrogen bonds in 9.0 g of ice. (b) Calculate the number of hydrogen bonds in 10.0 g of liquid HF. (c) Use your answers to explain why water has a higher boiling point than HF even though fluorine is more electronegative than oxygen. (d) Explain why ice is less dense than liquid water.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) $M_r(\mathrm{H_2O}) = 2\times1.0 + 16.0 = 18.0$, so $n = 9.0 / 18.0 = 0.50\ \mathrm{mol}$. Bonds per molecule $= 4/2 = 2$. Amount of bonds $= 0.50\times2 = 1.0\ \mathrm{mol}$; number $= 1.0\times6.02\times10^{23} = $ **$6.02\times10^{23}$ hydrogen bonds**.

(b) $M_r(\mathrm{HF}) = 1.0 + 19.0 = 20.0$, so $n = 10.0 / 20.0 = 0.50\ \mathrm{mol}$. Bonds per molecule $= 2/2 = 1$. Amount of bonds $= 0.50\ \mathrm{mol}$; number $= 0.50\times6.02\times10^{23} = $ **$3.01\times10^{23}$ hydrogen bonds**.

(c) Per mole of substance water has 2 mol of hydrogen bonds and HF only 1 mol. Each H-F bond is individually stronger, but water has two hydrogens and two lone pairs per molecule, so it forms twice as many bonds; more energy is needed to separate its molecules, so its boiling point is higher.

(d) In ice each molecule is held by four hydrogen bonds in an open, regular lattice with empty spaces. On melting, some hydrogen bonds break and the molecules move closer together, so the same mass occupies a smaller volume and liquid water is denser than ice.

items_markdown: A hydrogen bond is an intermolecular attraction between an H atom bonded to N, O or F and a lone pair on N, O or F of another molecule; it is not a covalent bond.
Before claiming hydrogen bonding, check for an N-H, O-H or F-H bond (donor) and a lone pair on N, O or F (acceptor).
Hydrogen bonds explain the anomalously high boiling points of NH3, H2O and HF compared with the other hydrides of their groups.
With similar relative molecular mass the order is: alkane or ether < amine < alcohol < carboxylic acid, because the strength of the strongest intermolecular force increases in that order.
Water has the highest boiling point of the group 16 and 17 hydrides because it forms about two hydrogen bonds per molecule; ice floats because its hydrogen-bonded lattice is open.
